![](./cover.png){fig-alt="Cover card reading From Dataset to a Biological Signature, over a solid purple background."}

Two acute leukemias arrive at the clinic looking much the same. Both fill the marrow
with immature white cells, both make the patient acutely ill within weeks, and under
a microscope the blasts of one can pass for the blasts of the other. They need
opposite treatments. Get it wrong and you give a toxic regimen that will not work to
someone who has a few weeks to spare.

Before 1999 that call was made by a blood specialist looking down a microscope at the
shape of the cells, at how they took up various dyes, and at which proteins sat on
their surface. It was good, and two hospitals could reach two answers. Golub and
colleagues asked whether the cells' gene activity could make the call on its own — and
whether you could have found the two diseases in the data without being told they
existed.

This post runs that question end to end, twice. The argument underneath it is one
sentence: **a signature only exists relative to a question you asked, and every number
you attach to one is shaped by the fact that the data itself picked the genes.** A
machine learning scientist and a statistician say that in different words; both
versions are here, and they are the same pipeline. For the concept without the code,
[What is a Biological Signature?](../what-is-a-biological-signature/) is the primer.

### Two assembly lines, and a glitch on one of them

The biology is worth two minutes, because it turns out to be what the model recovers.
Think of bone marrow as a factory with two assembly lines running from a single stem
cell. The **lymphoid** line builds the immune system's sharpshooters, B-cells and
T-cells. The **myeloid** line builds everything else: red cells that carry oxygen,
platelets that clot, and the white cells that do the frontline brawling.

An acute leukemia is a glitch that jams one line. The marrow fills with cells caught
half-built — blasts — that will neither finish growing into anything useful nor stop
dividing.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  S["Bone marrow stem cell"] --> L["Lymphoid line<br/>B-cells, T-cells"]
  S --> M["Myeloid line<br/>red cells, platelets, granulocytes"]
  L -->|glitch| ALL["<b>ALL</b><br/>lymphoblasts"]
  M -->|glitch| AML["<b>AML</b><br/>myeloblasts"]
```

Jam the lymphoid line and you get acute lymphoblastic leukemia, ALL — the commonest
cancer of childhood. Jam the myeloid line and you get acute myeloid leukemia, AML,
mostly an adult disease, and faster to strip out oxygen transport and clotting because
the myeloid line covers more jobs.

So the diagnostic question has a clean biological shape: *which line is stuck?* Hold
on to that. It is what the classifier ends up measuring.

### The data, and who went to the trouble of collecting it

The measurements come from Golub et al. (1999) at the Whitehead Institute and
Dana-Farber, who took marrow and blood from 72 acute leukemia patients and ran each
sample over an Affymetrix HU6800 array: a glass chip carrying 7,129 tiny patches, each
keyed to one gene. Sample material sticks to the patch that matches it and glows, so a
bright spot means that gene was busy in that patient. They were not building a
product; they pulled samples from hospital archives to argue that a tumour's type is
legible in gene activity at all.

A decision made from this analysis is a treatment assignment: vincristine and
steroids for ALL, cytarabine and an anthracycline for AML, for a patient seriously
ill either way. So the interesting number is not peak accuracy. It is how much of the
accuracy survives being carried to a different hospital.

I use the copy on Efron and Hastie's *Computer Age Statistical Inference* data page,
cached in this post's `data/` directory so the render never touches the network.

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Imports, plot style, and loading the cached matrices"

import warnings
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import beta

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
rng_seed = 0

plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 150, "savefig.bbox": "tight", "font.size": 9,
    "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.25, "axes.axisbelow": True,
})
ALL_C, AML_C = "#1D5C6E", "#C98A12"

# The CASI matrix: 7,128 genes x 72 samples, column names carry the labels.
casi = pd.read_csv("data/leukemia_big.csv.gz")
X = casi.to_numpy().T                                    # samples x genes
y = np.array([int(c.split(".")[0].startswith("AML")) for c in casi.columns])

# The original Whitehead files, used only as a key: they carry the Affymetrix
# probe accessions and the per-patient sample IDs that the CASI copy dropped.
def read_golub(path):
    d = pd.read_csv(path)
    ids = [c for c in d.columns[2:] if not c.startswith("call")]
    return d["Gene Accession Number"].to_numpy(), d["Gene Description"].to_numpy(), \
           d[ids].to_numpy(dtype=float), ids

acc, desc, G_train, id_train = read_golub("data/golub_train.csv.gz")
_, _, G_test, id_test = read_golub("data/golub_independent.csv.gz")
truth = pd.read_csv("data/golub_labels.csv").set_index("patient")["cancer"].to_dict()

print(f"expression matrix : {X.shape[0]} samples x {X.shape[1]} genes")
print(f"class balance     : {(y==0).sum()} ALL, {y.sum()} AML")
```

Seventy-two samples, 7,128 genes. That is a hundred times more things measured than
people to measure them on, and every difficulty below follows from that one ratio.

```{python}
#| label: slice
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "A corner of the matrix"

pd.DataFrame(
    X[:5, :6].round(3),
    index=[f"sample {i} ({'AML' if y[i] else 'ALL'})" for i in range(5)],
    columns=[f"gene {j}" for j in range(6)],
)
```

These are not raw brightness readings. Each *column* — each patient — has been
rescaled so their 7,128 values average zero with a spread of one, which puts every
patient on the same footing however bright their chip came out. Something was done to
each gene across patients too, but the file's own documentation says that step is
"lost in time".

## The file on Hastie's server holds Golub's two groups, stored backwards

Golub's design had a feature that matters more than anything else here. The 72 samples
are not one pool. Thirty-eight came from a single hospital, all bone marrow, and those
built the predictor. The other 34 were collected later at different reference
laboratories, prepared by different hands to different recipes, some of them blood
rather than marrow. That second group differs from the training set in exactly the
ways a new hospital would — which is the only kind of test set whose score is worth
quoting.

The file I am using has no patient identifiers, so that split looks lost. It is
recoverable, and worth recovering properly rather than guessing from class counts.
Here is the lever: rescaling a patient's column stretches and shifts their numbers but
cannot reorder them, so the gene that was third-brightest before is third-brightest
after. That surviving order is as good as a fingerprint. Replace every value by its
rank within its column, then see which column of one file moves with which column of
the other. Correlating ranks rather than values is what makes this a Spearman
correlation.

```{python}
#| label: recover-split
#| code-fold: show

G = np.hstack([G_train, G_test])[:X.shape[1]]   # CASI drops Golub's last probe
ids = id_train + id_test
golub_y = np.array([int(truth[int(i)] == "AML") for i in ids])

rank = lambda A: np.argsort(np.argsort(A, axis=0), axis=0).astype(float)
Rc, Rg = rank(casi.to_numpy()), rank(G)
Rc = (Rc - Rc.mean(0)) / Rc.std(0)
Rg = (Rg - Rg.mean(0)) / Rg.std(0)
S = (Rc.T @ Rg) / G.shape[0]                    # 72 x 72 Spearman matrix
match, best = S.argmax(1), np.sort(S, axis=1)

print(f"unique matches      : {len(set(match.tolist()))}/72")
print(f"labels agree        : {(golub_y[match] == y).sum()}/72")
print(f"worst true match    : {best[:, -1].min():.3f}")
print(f"best runner-up      : {best[:, -2].max():.3f}")
print(f"CASI column 0 -> patient {ids[match[0]]};  column 34 -> patient {ids[match[34]]}")
```

Every column matches exactly one patient, none is claimed twice, and every recovered
label agrees. The weakest true match scores 0.945 while the best wrong candidate
anywhere reaches 0.884, so nothing here is close. It also settles the ordering: column
0 is patient 39 and column 34 is patient 1, so the file stores the **34 outside
samples first**. Slice it at the front expecting training data and you get Golub's
held-out patients instead.

One caveat no amount of later care removes. That undocumented per-gene step may well
have been computed across all 72 patients at once. Rescaling a patient's own column is
safe, since it only ever looks at itself; a step that pools every patient is not,
because it lets the 34 test samples touch the training data before the split.
Everything below is conditional on it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-data
#| fig-cap: "Left: two genes named later in the post, one myeloid and one lymphoid, separate the classes almost on their own. Right: the component that carries diagnosis plotted against the one that carries cohort. Class separates left-to-right and the laboratory separates bottom-to-top, on different axes — the nuisance variable has structure of its own."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure 1"

test_ix, train_ix = np.arange(34), np.arange(34, 72)
probe = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(acc[:X.shape[1]])}
mpo, ccnd3 = probe["M19507_at"], probe["M92287_at"]

Z = (X - X.mean(0)) / (X.std(0) + 1e-9)
U, sv, _ = np.linalg.svd(Z - Z.mean(0), full_matrices=False)
pcs = U[:, :5] * sv[:5]

# Pick the axes by what they actually carry, rather than assuming PC1/PC2:
# correlate each component with class and with cohort membership.
cohort = np.r_[np.zeros(34), np.ones(38)]
corr = lambda v: np.array([abs(np.corrcoef(v, pcs[:, k])[0, 1]) for k in range(5)])
k_cls, k_coh = corr(y).argmax(), corr(cohort).argmax()

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.6))
for cls, name, col in [(0, "ALL", ALL_C), (1, "AML", AML_C)]:
    m = y == cls
    a1.scatter(X[m, ccnd3], X[m, mpo], c=col, s=28, alpha=0.85, label=name,
               edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5)
a1.set(xlabel="CCND3 (cyclin D3), lymphoid", ylabel="MPO (myeloperoxidase), myeloid",
       title="Two genes")
a1.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)

for cls, col in [(0, ALL_C), (1, AML_C)]:
    for ix, mark, lab in [(train_ix, "o", "training"), (test_ix, "^", "external")]:
        m = np.intersect1d(np.flatnonzero(y == cls), ix)
        a2.scatter(pcs[m, k_cls], pcs[m, k_coh], c=col, marker=mark, s=28, alpha=0.85,
                   edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5,
                   label=f"{'AML' if cls else 'ALL'}, {lab}")
a2.set(xlabel=f"PC{k_cls + 1}  (carries class, |r| = {corr(y)[k_cls]:.2f})",
       ylabel=f"PC{k_coh + 1}  (carries cohort, |r| = {corr(cohort)[k_coh]:.2f})",
       title="Colour = class, shape = cohort")
a2.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=7, loc="best")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Two hand-picked genes almost draw the line on their own, which tells you the signal
here is unusually strong. Hold on to that when the error rates arrive.

The right panel is the warning attached to it. Take the cloud of patients in 7,128
dimensions and ask which single direction through it spreads them out most, then which
does so among what is left, and so on; those directions are the principal components.
Here the direction tracking the diagnosis and the direction tracking which of the two
collection batches a sample belongs to are two *different* components. The batch is not
a fog of random error over the disease signal — it is its own clean pattern at its own
angle. Train a ridge classifier to guess only the batch, telling it nothing about the
diagnosis, and cross-validation puts it at 78%. A model will learn that, because it is
there to be learnt.

## For the ML scientist: the biology is all upstream of the matrix

**What does the model actually see?** A table: one row per patient, one column per
gene, one number in each cell. Every piece of biology sits upstream of it — which
patch stands for which gene, what to do with readings too dim or too bright to trust,
how to put different chips on a comparable scale. All of it is specific to this assay
and travels nowhere; redo the study on today's sequencing and every choice changes,
while the table coming out looks the same. After the table it is ordinary supervised
learning. That lopsidedness is why genomics pipelines break when they are moved rather
than when they are built.

**So is finding a signature supervised or unsupervised?** Supervised, and worth saying
flatly, because the field's vocabulary blurs it. A signature is only defined against a
question — sick or well, this tumour or that one. Take the labels away and the data
still has structure, but structure is not a signature. It is a pattern that might be
the disease, or the patients' sex, or the laboratory, or the day the samples were run.
Methods that work without labels do the supporting work, including the check that the
biggest patterns are biology rather than paperwork — which is what the right panel was
for.

There is a real exception, and Golub's paper is why it is famous. Cluster first, find
a grouping nobody had a name for, then treat those groups as if they were labels and
go looking for what separates them. That is class *discovery*, and their paper did
both halves. Discovery proposes the question; answering it is still supervised.

**What actually ships to a hospital?** Not a model somebody keeps tuning: a fixed list
of genes, a fixed weight for each, and a fixed cut-off, all locked before anyone opens
the test set. Which is why the penalty below is set by testing inside the training
data, never by trying values against the test set and keeping the best:

$$
\hat\beta \;=\; \arg\min_{\beta}\; -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[y_i\,x_i^{\top}\beta - \log\big(1 + e^{x_i^{\top}\beta}\big)\Big] \;+\; \lambda\Big(\alpha\lVert\beta\rVert_1 + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\lVert\beta\rVert_2^2\Big)
$$

Read it as two demands pulling against each other. The first part rewards fitting the
patients you have. The part after the plus sign charges for weight put on genes, in two
currencies. The first, $\lVert\beta\rVert_1$, charges by the plain size of a weight. That charge
has a sharp corner at zero, and the corner is the whole point: it makes an exact zero
the best answer for a gene even when some small non-zero weight would fit the patients
slightly better. So genes drop out completely and a short list survives. The second,
$\lVert\beta\rVert_2^2$, charges by the *square* of a weight, which is smooth at zero
and so shrinks weights without ever quite reaching it. What it does instead is punish
one big weight far more than two medium ones, so genes that rise and fall together end
up sharing the credit rather than one being kept at random and its twins discarded.
Together they are the elastic net. Fixing $\alpha = 0.5$ keeps both charges in play and
leaves a single dial: $\lambda$, how expensive genes are in total.

Setting that dial needs care, because data used to choose it has helped build the
model and can no longer judge it. So choosing and judging get separate patients. Split
the 38 into five groups; hold one out; inside the other four run a smaller split that
tries each candidate penalty and keeps the winner. (The code and the figure below turn
the dial by its reciprocal, $C$, so larger $C$ means a *weaker* penalty.) Only then is the held-out group
spent, scoring a model whose dial it had no hand in setting. Rotate through all five
and average. An inner loop that chooses, an outer loop that scores: nested
cross-validation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-path
#| fig-cap: "Inner-fold accuracy along the regularisation path, on the 38 training samples only. Accuracy peaks at a single interior value. To the left the penalty is strong enough to zero out genes the model needs; to the right it is weak enough to admit genes that only help on the training fold. Error bars are one standard deviation across five folds, and they are wide — 38 samples do not locate this optimum precisely."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Nested cross-validation, and Figure 2"

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, roc_auc_score, brier_score_loss

Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte = X[train_ix], y[train_ix], X[test_ix], y[test_ix]
Cs = np.logspace(-2, 1, 7)

def enet(C):
    return LogisticRegression(penalty="elasticnet", solver="saga", l1_ratio=0.5,
                              C=C, max_iter=3000, tol=1e-3, random_state=rng_seed)

def screen(A, k=2000):
    """Unsupervised variance screen. Never sees y, so it is safe inside a fold."""
    return np.argsort(-A.var(0))[:k]

outer, scores = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0), []
for a, b in outer.split(Xtr, ytr):
    g = screen(Xtr[a])
    mu, sd = Xtr[a][:, g].mean(0), Xtr[a][:, g].std(0) + 1e-9
    Za, Zb = (Xtr[a][:, g] - mu) / sd, (Xtr[b][:, g] - mu) / sd
    inner = StratifiedKFold(4, shuffle=True, random_state=1)
    C = max(Cs, key=lambda c: cross_val_score(enet(c), Za, ytr[a], cv=inner).mean())
    scores.append(accuracy_score(ytr[b], enet(C).fit(Za, ytr[a]).predict(Zb)))

# Full-training-set path, for the figure and for the final penalty.
g = screen(Xtr)
mu, sd = Xtr[:, g].mean(0), Xtr[:, g].std(0) + 1e-9
Ztr, Zte = (Xtr[:, g] - mu) / sd, (Xte[:, g] - mu) / sd
cv5 = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=1)
path = np.array([cross_val_score(enet(c), Ztr, ytr, cv=cv5) for c in Cs])
C_star = Cs[path.mean(1).argmax()]

print(f"nested CV accuracy : {np.mean(scores):.3f}  (outer folds "
      f"{[round(s, 2) for s in scores]})")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.2))
ax.errorbar(Cs, path.mean(1), yerr=path.std(1), marker="o", color=ALL_C,
            capsize=3, linewidth=1.5, markersize=5)
ax.axvline(C_star, color=AML_C, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.3,
           label=f"chosen C = {C_star:.2f}")
ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="C  (inverse penalty strength)",
       ylabel="inner-fold accuracy", title="Regularisation path")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.show()
```

That two-loop procedure puts the predictor at 0.921 accuracy on the training
patients. Now lock the gene list, the weights and the cut-off, and open the 34 outside
samples — once.

```{python}
#| label: external
#| code-fold: show

final = enet(C_star).fit(Ztr, ytr)
selected = g[np.flatnonzero(final.coef_[0])]
p_test = final.predict_proba(Zte)[:, 1]

print(f"genes with non-zero coefficient : {len(selected)}")
print(f"external accuracy : {accuracy_score(yte, p_test > 0.5):.3f} "
      f"({int((( p_test > 0.5) == yte).sum())}/34)")
print(f"external AUC      : {roc_auc_score(yte, p_test):.3f}")
print(f"external Brier    : {brier_score_loss(yte, p_test):.3f}")
wrong = np.flatnonzero((p_test > 0.5).astype(int) != yte)
print(f"the one error     : predicted p(AML) = {p_test[wrong][0]:.3f}")
```

**What did it find?** Thirty-three of the 34 outside samples correct. The AUC of 1.000
says that given any AML patient and any ALL patient, the model always gives the AML
patient the higher probability: it ranks all 34 correctly, even though the cut-off at
0.5 converts one of those rankings into a wrong answer. The Brier score averages the *squared*
gap between each quoted probability and what actually happened, and squaring is what
makes a confident mistake cost far more than a hesitant one. The single error sits at $p = 0.468$, three hundredths on the wrong side of the
line — the model was almost exactly undecided.

Note which way the gap runs. The training-only estimate said 0.921 and the outside
cohort delivered 0.971, so the internal number *understated* how well the model
travelled — the opposite of the failure everyone is trained to expect.

The gene list is what closes the loop back to the marrow.

```{python}
#| label: lineage
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Naming the selected genes"

lineage = {
    "M19507_at": "MPO, myeloperoxidase — the granulocyte enzyme",
    "M23197_at": "CD33 — myeloid surface antigen",
    "X52056_at": "SPI1 / PU.1 — myeloid master transcription factor",
    "M84526_at": "DF, adipsin — Golub's AML-high list",
    "M27891_at": "CST3, cystatin C — Golub's AML-high list",
    "M92287_at": "CCND3, cyclin D3 — Golub's ALL-high list",
    "U05259_rna1_at": "MB-1 / CD79a — B-cell receptor component",
    "M31523_at": "TCF3 / E2A — required for B-cell development",
}
hits = [(acc[i], lineage[acc[i]]) for i in selected if acc[i] in lineage]
for a, note in hits:
    print(f"  {a:16s} {note}")
print(f"\n{len(hits)} of these annotated markers survived selection.")
```

Myeloid markers on one side, lymphoid on the other. The model is reading out which
assembly line is stuck: it has rediscovered the question the biology poses, rather
than memorising 72 patients. And among the genes it keeps is myeloperoxidase — the
very enzyme the pre-1999 laboratory stain tested for. The gene activity arrives at the
specialist's own marker from the other direction.

That is the optimistic reading. The next section runs the same pipeline and asks what
those numbers are estimates *of*.

## For the statistician: the data chose the genes, and every number remembers that

Describe the same job in a statistician's words and the difficulty changes shape.
Statisticians write that hundred-to-one ratio as $p \gg n$ — far more things measured
than subjects to measure them on — and add a bet that only a handful of the 7,128
matter. The procedure then has to do two jobs at once: pick the handful, and report a
weight for each one it picked. Those jobs cannot be separated, and the second inherits
everything the first did.

That is why the usual confidence interval around a selected gene's weight means
nothing. Such an interval assumes the gene was named in advance. This one is in the
list *because* it looked good in these 38 patients — it won a contest against 7,127
rivals, and some of why it won is luck that will not repeat. Quote the interval anyway
and it comes out too narrow, the p-value beside it too small. Three honest repairs
exist: choose genes on one half of the patients and do all inference on the half never
consulted; work out what winning the contest does to the numbers and correct for it,
which is selective inference; or run fake genes that imitate the real correlation
structure but are known to be unrelated to the disease through the same contest, and
count how often a fake wins — knockoffs.

Then there is the sheer number of tests. Run 7,128 comparisons at the usual 5%
threshold and about 356 genes clear it by chance alone. The reflex fix — demand a far
stricter threshold on each test — throws away almost every real finding along with the
false ones at this scale. The guarantee people use instead is the false discovery
rate: not "how likely am I to make even one mistake", but "of the genes I report, what
fraction should I expect to be wrong",

$$
\mathrm{FDR} \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{V}{\max(R, 1)}\right],
$$

where $R$ counts the genes you reported and $V$ counts how many of those were wrong.
Setting that expected fraction to, say, 10% is a workable promise: a tenth of your
list is junk, on average, and you proceed knowing it.

The trouble is the phrase *on average*. Genes do not act independently; they come in
gangs that switch on and off together, so one upstream event drags fifty along and the
number of genuinely separate questions is far below 7,128. Benjamini–Hochberg still
delivers its long-run promise when genes move *together*, which is the common case
here; it is not guaranteed when a block moves in opposition, as repression produces. But the fraction you get
*this time* swings widely around it, precisely because genes move in gangs — one gang
going wrong takes fifty entries with it. You can control the average perfectly and
still hold a badly wrong list today.

Stated as stages, the pipeline the section above ran informally is:

1. Decide what you are estimating, and where the cut-off goes, before looking.
2. Split the data before any transformation touches it.
3. Fit rescaling and any gene filter on training data only, inside each fold.
4. Choose the penalty in an inner loop; measure performance in an outer one.
5. Check the gene set is stable, not merely best on one draw.
6. Lock the weights and cut-off, test outside once, and report intervals and how
   truthful the probabilities were — not one bare accuracy figure.

Step 3 is the one usually violated, and the violation is almost never deliberate.

### Cheating happens by default, because the gene filter looked at everything

The natural way to handle 7,128 genes is to score each on how cleanly it separates ALL
from AML, keep the best 50, and cross-validate on those. It feels safe: inside the loop
the model only ever trains on the training fold. But the scoring step ran once, over
all the data, before the loop started. So the fold you are holding back already had a
vote in choosing the genes it is about to score. Information has leaked across the
split, which is why this is called leakage. Ambroise and McLachlan named it in 2002,
and it reproduces in a few lines.

```{python}
#| label: leakage
#| code-fold: show

def top_genes(A, lab, k=50):
    m0, m1 = A[lab == 0].mean(0), A[lab == 1].mean(0)
    se = np.sqrt(A[lab == 0].var(0) / (lab == 0).sum()
                 + A[lab == 1].var(0) / lab.sum()) + 1e-9
    return np.argsort(-np.abs((m1 - m0) / se))[:k]

def two_ways(lab, cv=StratifiedKFold(10, shuffle=True, random_state=7)):
    once = cross_val_score(enet(1.0), Z[:, top_genes(Z, lab)], lab, cv=cv).mean()
    fold = [accuracy_score(lab[b], enet(1.0)
            .fit(Z[a][:, (gi := top_genes(Z[a], lab[a]))], lab[a])
            .predict(Z[b][:, gi])) for a, b in cv.split(Z, lab)]
    return 1 - once, 1 - np.mean(fold)

opt, honest = two_ways(y)
print(f"real labels     : filter once {opt:.1%} error | filter in fold {honest:.1%}")

shuffled = np.random.default_rng(3).permutation(y)
opt_n, honest_n = two_ways(shuffled)
print(f"labels shuffled : filter once {opt_n:.1%} error | filter in fold {honest_n:.1%}")
print(f"chance for this class balance : {(y == 0).mean():.1%} correct by always saying ALL")
```

On the real labels the gap is small — 2.9% error the cheating way against 4.3% done
properly — and that is the honest result, not a failed demonstration. The ALL/AML
difference is so stark that cheating has almost nothing left to add.

The second line is the demonstration. Shuffle the labels so there is genuinely nothing
to find, and picking the genes once over the whole dataset reports 7.0% error — 93%
accuracy on pure noise. Pick inside each fold instead and the error climbs to 33.2%,
about what you get by ignoring the data and calling everyone ALL — the cell prints that
as 65.3% correct, which is 34.7% error. So the
flattery is not a small bias that shrinks with the signal. With nothing there, the
flattery is the whole number: invisible when you do not need the estimate,
catastrophic when you do.

### The gene list is one draw, not the answer

Being the best list for these 38 patients is not the same as being a list that would
come back if you ran the study again. There is a cheap way to tell the difference.
Take a random half of the training patients, fit the same kind of model at one fixed
middling penalty, note which genes survived, then draw another random half — a hundred
times. A gene picked for a real biological
reason keeps reappearing; a gene picked because it flattered one particular set of
patients does not. Counting those reappearances is stability selection.

```{python}
#| label: fig-stability
#| fig-cap: "Selection frequency across 100 half-samples of the training cohort, sorted. The dashed line is a 0.6 cutoff. Genes above it are labelled by Affymetrix probe."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Stability selection, and Figure 3"

rng = np.random.default_rng(rng_seed)
freq, B = np.zeros(X.shape[1]), 100
pool = screen(Xtr)
for _ in range(B):
    take = rng.choice(len(ytr), len(ytr) // 2, replace=False)
    if len(np.unique(ytr[take])) < 2:
        continue
    A = Xtr[take][:, pool]
    A = (A - A.mean(0)) / (A.std(0) + 1e-9)
    freq[pool[np.flatnonzero(enet(0.5).fit(A, ytr[take]).coef_[0])]] += 1
freq /= B

order = np.argsort(-freq)
for t in (0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.9):
    print(f"selection frequency >= {t}: {(freq >= t).sum()} genes")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 3.4))
top = order[:60]
ax.bar(range(len(top)), freq[top], color=ALL_C, width=0.8)
ax.axhline(0.6, color=AML_C, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.3, label="cutoff = 0.6")
above = int((freq[top] >= 0.6).sum())
ax.set_xticks(range(above))
ax.set_xticklabels([acc[i] for i in top[:above]], rotation=90, fontsize=5)
ax.set(xlim=(-1, len(top)), ylabel="selection frequency",
       xlabel="genes, ranked", title=f"{B} half-samples of the 38 training patients")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.show()
```

Forty-five genes turn up in at least half the draws, and only 12 in nine draws out of
ten. These runs hold the penalty fixed instead of retuning it each time, so they
measure how steady this kind of selection is rather than re-deriving the shipped
88-gene list exactly. The lesson transfers to it regardless: a list built this way is
not a single settled object. Most of its members could be swapped for a neighbour that
rises and falls with them, and a different 38 patients would have handed back a visibly
different list with much the same accuracy.

That wobble is not something the elastic net introduced. Rebuild Golub's own 50-gene
predictor with the score from his paper — the gap between the two group averages
divided by how much the groups scatter, $P(g,c) = (\mu_1 - \mu_0)/(\sigma_1 +
\sigma_0)$ — then compute the identical score after the tidying step his methods
section mentions in passing: pull readings below 100 up to 100 and above 16,000 down
to 16,000, then take logarithms.

```{python}
#| label: golub50
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Reconstructing the 1999 predictor"

def snr(A, lab):
    d = A[lab == 1].mean(0) - A[lab == 0].mean(0)
    return d / (A[lab == 1].std(0, ddof=1) + A[lab == 0].std(0, ddof=1) + 1e-12)

raw = G_train.T
P_raw = snr(raw, golub_y[:38])
P_log = snr(np.log10(np.clip(raw, 100, 16000)), golub_y[:38])
fifty = lambda P: set(np.argsort(-P)[:25]) | set(np.argsort(P)[:25])
g50_raw, g50_log = fifty(P_raw), fifty(P_log)

print(f"Golub-50, raw vs his own log10 preprocessing : {len(g50_raw & g50_log)}/50 shared")
print(f"elastic net set vs Golub-50 (log10)         : "
      f"{len(set(selected) & g50_log)} of 50 genes in common")
print("top AML-high probes:",
      ", ".join(acc[i] for i in np.argsort(-P_log)[:4]))
```

His top 50 changes by 18 genes on that one choice, with the patients, the data and the
scoring rule all held fixed. Against that backdrop the elastic net agreeing with him on
26 of 50 is neither a failure to replicate nor a confirmation — it is what two
reasonable ways of choosing agree on when the thing chosen is this wobbly. The gene
list is an estimate, like an average or a slope, and estimates come with a spread.

## Closing: 34 patients cannot tell you how well this works

The outside cohort did what it was supposed to do. Collected somewhere else, prepared
differently, and including a tissue the training set never contained — and the locked
model still got 33 of 34 right. That is a real result, and Golub designing that split
in advance is why it means anything at all.

But 34 is 34.

```{python}
#| label: closing
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Intervals, and what happens at a different prevalence"

def wilson(k, n, z=1.96):
    c = (k / n + z * z / (2 * n)) / (1 + z * z / n)
    h = z * np.sqrt(k / n * (1 - k / n) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n)) / (1 + z * z / n)
    return c - h, c + h

print(f"external accuracy 33/34   : 95% CI [{wilson(33, 34)[0]:.3f}, {wilson(33, 34)[1]:.3f}]")
print(f"nested CV, 35/38          : 95% CI [{wilson(35, 38)[0]:.3f}, {wilson(35, 38)[1]:.3f}]")

sens, fpr_hi = 13 / 14, beta.ppf(0.975, 1, 20)
print(f"\nspecificity 20/20, but 95% upper bound on the false-positive rate: {fpr_hi:.3f}")
for prev, where in [(0.35, "suspected leukemia at referral"), (0.02, "a broader haematology clinic")]:
    ppv = sens * prev / (sens * prev + fpr_hi * (1 - prev))
    print(f"  prevalence {prev:>5.0%} ({where}): PPV could be as low as {ppv:.2f}")
```

Thirty-three out of 34 is 0.971, but the honest range around it — the set of true
accuracies that could plausibly have produced this result — runs from 0.851 to 0.995.
A model that really gets 30 of 34 right would look no different on evidence this thin.

The same thinness hides on the other side. The model never once called an ALL patient
AML — 20 out of 20 — which looks like perfection. But no mistakes in twenty attempts
is still consistent with a true error rate near 17%, and that bound is what travels.
Push it through the arithmetic of who is being tested, using that bound in place of
the flawless score. Among patients already referred with suspected leukemia, about a
third of whom have AML, a positive call comes out right about three times in four. Take
the same model to a broader haematology clinic where only one leukemia patient in fifty
has AML, and the same figure drops to about one time in ten — most positive answers
wrong, because nearly everyone it meets has the other disease. Only the false-alarm
rate is being held at its pessimistic bound here; the hit rate stays at the 13 of 14
actually observed. So these are not true worst cases. They are what twenty clean calls
on the other side fail to rule out. Note what this arithmetic does *not* cover. Every error rate here was measured on
people who already had one of these two leukemias, so none of it says what the model
would do when handed someone who has neither.

Which returns to the sentence at the top. A signature is defined against a question,
and also against the population you asked it in. Accuracy is not a property of the
model. It is a property of the model pointed at a particular group of people. Golub's
predictor answers "which of these two leukemias does this patient have" for a patient
who already has one of them. Point it at a population where AML is rare and the
arithmetic above, not the classifier, decides what it is worth.
